cues.text: Welcome back.
What connects a falling ball with a satellite above Earth?
Both accelerate because of gravity.
The satellite has enough sideways motion to keep falling around Earth instead
of reaching the surface.
We will build that idea carefully.
Newton's gravitational law says the attractive force between two point masses
equals capital G times the two masses, divided by the square of their
separation.
Capital G is the universal gravitational constant.
It is not the same as little g, the gravitational acceleration at a particular
place.
For an object outside a spherically symmetric planet, the planet attracts it as
though the planet's mass were at its centre.
That means the distance in the denominator is measured from the centre, not
from the surface.
Here is a quick ratio problem.
Keep both masses fixed and double their separation.
What happens to the force?
Take a moment.
The denominator becomes four times larger, so the force becomes one quarter as
large.
If one mass also doubles, the new force is half the original force.
Ratios often save time in JEE problems.
Finally, the two bodies feel equal and opposite gravitational forces, but their
accelerations need not be equal because their masses differ.
Now divide the gravitational force on a small object by its mass.
The mass cancels, leaving little g equal to capital G times the planet's mass
divided by distance from the centre squared.
This explains why different objects have the same gravitational acceleration at
the same location when we neglect air resistance and other forces.
Let Earth's radius be capital R and the object's height above the surface be h.
Its distance from Earth's centre is R plus h.
Compare gravity there with gravity at the surface: the ratio is R divided by R
plus h, all squared.
Suppose the height equals one Earth radius.
Is gravity half its surface value?
Pause before answering.
The centre distance is two R, so gravity is one quarter, not one half.
If the surface value is ten metres per second squared in a problem, the new
value is two point five.
A two kilogram object then has gravitational force five newtons, while its mass
remains two kilograms.
These equations use a spherical, nonrotating planet model.
Do not use the exterior inverse square formula inside Earth by simply inserting
a smaller radius.
The mass distribution inside the chosen radius matters there.
Our energy lesson used m g h near Earth's surface.
For large changes in distance, gravity is not constant, so we need a more
general expression.
Choose gravitational potential energy to be zero infinitely far from an
isolated planet.
At distance r outside that planet, the potential energy of the planet and
object system is minus capital G times M times m divided by r.
Why negative?
You must supply energy to separate the initially stationary masses to infinity.
Their initial energy is therefore below the zero level chosen there.
Negative does not mean impossible or unphysical; it reflects the reference
level.
Let us move an object from radius R to radius two R.
Initially the energy is minus G M m over R.
Finally it is minus G M m over two R.
Final minus initial gives a positive increase, G M m over two R.
Moving outward makes the energy less negative.
If you lift the object slowly with negligible change in kinetic energy, your
work equals that increase, and gravity does the opposite work.
For a small height compared with the planet's radius, this change is
approximately m g h using surface g.
Always distinguish potential energy from gravitational potential, which is
potential energy per unit mass.
Picture a satellite moving in a circular orbit around a much more massive
planet.
Its speed can stay constant while its velocity changes, because the direction
keeps turning.
Gravity provides the inward acceleration.
There is no extra centripetal force to add to gravity: centripetal describes
the role of the net inward force.
Equate G M m over r squared to m v squared over r.
Cancel the satellite mass and one factor of r.
The result is v squared equals G M over r, so circular orbital speed is the
square root of G M over r.
A larger circular orbit has a lower speed.
For an ideal planet with surface gravity ten metres per second squared and
radius six point four million metres, G M equals surface g times R squared.
The formal circular speed at radius R is therefore the square root of g R:
eight thousand metres per second.
At four R it is four thousand metres per second.
These are ideal model values, not instructions for flying at the surface.
The orbital period is circumference divided by speed, giving two pi times the
square root of r cubed over G M.
Increasing radius fourfold makes the period eight times longer.
Astronauts feel weightless because they and their spacecraft are in free fall
together, not because gravity has disappeared.
How fast must an object start to escape an isolated planet without further
propulsion?
Use energy, and neglect atmosphere, planet rotation, and other celestial
bodies.
At the minimum escape speed, the object approaches infinity with its speed
tending to zero.
Its final total mechanical energy is zero.
Initially, kinetic energy plus gravitational potential energy must also be
zero.
One half m v squared minus G M m over r equals zero.
Solving gives escape speed equal to the square root of two G M over r.
The object's mass cancels.
Compare this with circular speed at the same radius: escape speed is the square
root of two times circular speed.
For our ideal planet, the circular speed at radius R was eight kilometres per
second.
Multiply by approximately one point four one four to get about eleven point
three kilometres per second.
Try a comparison: a planet has the same radius but four times the mass.
Its escape speed doubles, because speed depends on the square root of mass.
Escape does not mean gravity suddenly switches off at a boundary.
Gravity weakens continuously as the object moves away.
Our result is an energy threshold for an unpowered departure, not a rule that
every powered rocket must reach that speed immediately.
Finish by checking centre distance, your planet model, and whether the question
asks for force, orbital speed, period, or escape speed.
